title: Pressure-Volume Work
lead: Work is a force integrated along a path. For a gas pushing on a piston the force comes from pressure, which leads to pressure-volume work and to the sign convention used for heat and work.
notes: Figures 19.2.1, 19.2.2 and 19.2.3 are shown together as one piston beside its PV diagram.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercises for this section; the one exercise, on compressing a gas against a constant pressure, was written by AI with an AI solution, and its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: A piston with internal pressure $P$ and external pressure $P_\text{ext}$. Pistons showing a compression (left) and an expansion (right). A system is compressed under constant external pressure, $P_\text{ext}$, from state 1 to state 2. The shaded area shows the amount of work being done for the compression. The dash-dot line is an isotherm, a path of constant temperature, showing that the initial and final temperature of the irreversible compression are the same.

exercises.prompt: 1.00 mol of an ideal gas is compressed from 10.0 L to 5.0 L against a constant external pressure of 2.00 bar. How much work is done on the gas?

answer.hint: Use $w = -P_\text{ext}\Delta V$ with the pressure in pascals and the volumes in cubic metres.
answer.solution: $\Delta V = 5.0\ \text{L} - 10.0\ \text{L} = -5.0\ \text{L} = -5.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$, and $P_\text{ext} = 2.00\times10^{5}$ Pa. Then $w = -P_\text{ext}\Delta V = -(2.00\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa})(-5.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3) = +1.00\times10^{3}$ J, or +1.00 kJ. The sign is positive because the surroundings put the energy into the gas as they compress it.

derivations.what: the work against a constant external pressure

assumes.text: The pressure that pushes on the piston from outside, $P_\text{ext}$, is the pressure exerted on the system, so it sets the work.

steps.cap: A constant pressure comes out of the integral.
